item.title: TornadoVM 7 Enables GPU-Native Workloads From Java Applications
item.description:
TornadoVM, an open-source heterogeneous programming framework for Java has reached version 7.0. It automatically accelerates Java programs on multi-core CPUs and GPUs and provides a rich GPU programming ecosystem in Java that can be used with any mainstream JDK distribution e.g. Temurin, Red Hat OpenJDK, Coretto, Oracle, GraalVM or Zulu.

By Ben Evans

item.title: US bans DeepSeek across federal agencies, putting AI supply chains under scrutiny
item.description:
DeepSeek has been dealt a huge blow in the US, even as it continues to innovate and keep pace with, or in some cases outperform, rival models from American labs.

The US Secretary of Homeland Security has issued an order banning all DeepSeek products and services from federal agencies. Government organizations must purge their IT systems of it within 60 days; those with “compelling justification” can make a case for exemption by written request to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) cited multiple concerns about the Chinese-hosted model, including data sovereignty, lax Chinese laws, and security vulnerabilities.

Analyst Erik Avakian, technical counselor at Infotech, understands the concern. “When organizations use any type of hosted AI service, they’re potentially sending intellectual property, confidential business information, or other sensitive data into an environment where they may have very little visibility or control over what happens to it,” he said.

Government concerns

According to a document published in the US Federal Register, all technology developed by China-based Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. will be banned from procurement by federal civilian agencies. This includes affiliated products and any third-party tools or software built using DeepSeek implementations.

Affected civilian executive branch agencies include the Departments of Treasury, State, and Justice; it does not apply, however, to private consumers, the general public, state/local governments, or Department of Defense (DoD) national security systems.

“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” the Order stated. To begin with, the company’s servers are located in the People’ s Republic of China (PRC), whose legal system grants “extensive authority” to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private infrastructure.

DeepSeek’s account generation process collects personally identifiable information (PII) and may also track and digitally fingerprint users, the Order asserted. Its prompt response process may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC. This could give it “actionable intelligence” on US programs or individual users.

Further, the Order stated, DeepSeek models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities. DHS pointed to open-source security research published in February 2025 that uncovered many iOS mobile apps with multiple critical vulnerabilities.

Until the ban takes full effect, DHS advised agencies to mitigate risk by monitoring inbound and outbound data traffic, implementing enhanced logging and controls on data exfiltration, and detecting and flagging anomalous activity.

Agencies can submit requests for exceptions to the ban in writing, and must provide a “compelling justification,” such as its impact on mission-critical functions, or other considerations related to national interest such as national security reviews, investigations, or security agreements, as reasons why such exemption should be granted,.

Security issues are rampant

The ban comes just as DeepSeek is open-sourcing DeepInfer, its in-house interference framework. DeepInfer powers DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with what the company said is high throughput and low latency. It features high-performance kernels, an optimized inference engine, structured outputs, and speculative decoding.

DeepSeek said its production token encoding and decoding components, which are aligned with processing logic behind the DeepSeek API, will bring the “same API behavior to community deployments.”

“Open models. Open kernels. Open inference,” DeepSeek posted to social media site X. “From private deployments to public clouds, we’ll keep working with the community to make large-scale inference more efficient.”

This isn’t its first roadblock from a cybersecurity perspective. Most notably, in January 2025, the company leaked more than one million log entries, including chat histories, API secrets, and other sensitive information, through an unsecured database.

DeepSeek reportedly addressed the exposure, but it still raised questions about the overall security practices surrounding the platform, particularly for organizations considering entrusting it with their own sensitive business information, Avakian pointed out.

That’s not to imply that every DeepSeek model is “inherently malicious,” he said, but there are still major questions around data privacy, the potential for information access under Chinese laws, the security of the broader AI ecosystem, and the susceptibility of DeepSeek’s models to jailbreaks and manipulation.

“Taken together, [these issues] raise legitimate concerns about whether organizations can adequately understand and manage the risks involved,” Avakian said.

Enterprises should seriously assess associated risk

Enterprises are increasingly exploring DeepSeek, although most publicly-documented adoption has been in China, Avakian noted. Some DeepSeek models have also been made available through platforms like Microsoft Azure and AWS.

“There’s genuine enterprise interest in the technology, as organizations look for opportunities to improve productivity, offer new capabilities, or reduce costs,” Avakian said. Useful applications include document summarization, internal research, and coding assistance.

DeepInfer also has the potential to reduce costs, but possible benefits should be weighed against associated security risks, he pointed out. The framework was just released, so organizations are going to need to validate the claimed efficiencies in their own environments rather than assuming savings will automatically translate into lower operating costs.

He encouraged organizations to start with relatively low-risk use cases, preferably using “public, synthetic, or appropriately sanitized information,” within a sandboxed environment they control themselves.

The important question to ask: ‘What is the business problem we’re trying to solve?’ From there, Avakian said, determine whether DeepSeek is the best way to solve it, validate security controls, and expand the use cases based on risk tolerance. Effective governance and risk assessment are key, he noted: understand what you’re bringing into your environment, validate its security, restrict its permissions, and make sure you can monitor what it’s doing.

“Approach this like any other software supply chain decision,” Avakian advised. “The fact that something is open source, inexpensive, or technically impressive doesn’t automatically make it appropriate for enterprise use.”

Impact on the broader AI ecosystem

The fact that the Order also addressed third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations is important, Avakian said, because organizations may be using DeepSeek technologies indirectly, through vendors, software platforms, or other services, without necessarily knowing what’s operating underneath. “These are classic supply chain issues,” he observed.

It’s no longer enough to know which AI applications employees are using; enterprises must understand which models, frameworks, dependencies, and external services are embedded in products they’re purchasing and deploying, Avakian said. This means revisiting AI inventories, potentially updating procurement requirements, and expanding processes around third-party risk management, he advised.

“Ultimately, enterprises leveraging these tools need to understand not only the AI technologies they’re intentionally deploying, but also the technologies they’re inheriting through third parties,” he said.

item.title: UK FCA exec wants to require disclosure of ‘significant AI failures and near-misses’
item.description:
When UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Chief Data Officer Jessica Rusu gave a speech on Monday advocating that UK companies be required to report “significant AI failures and near-misses,” she added to the drumbeat of demands for some kind of regulatory control over enterprise AI deployments. 

But her speech also highlighted regulator frustration over futile attempts to slow down the seemingly unstoppable agentic and genAI rollouts, as reports of agent misbehavior and the lack of meaningful consequences continue to emerge with alarming frequency.

Rusu, speaking to a Bloomberg UK Policy Series audience, said that firms need to invest more in cyber and operational resilience.

“Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognized, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too,” Rusu said. “It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress, or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.”

She added, “the FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators, and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.”

One of the questions that came out of the speech is what precisely was meant by “significant AI failures and near-misses.” Questions to FCA to clarify their terminology were not answered by publication time.

AI failure vs near miss

But Pieter Arntz, a malware intelligence researcher at security firm Malwarebytes, offered his own take on what those terms likely mean.

“A significant AI failure is one with serious consequences, not simply an incorrect answer. In financial services, that could mean an AI system authorizing substantial fraudulent payments, exposing sensitive customer information, denying customers access to essential financial services, or triggering transactions that threaten market integrity,” Arntz said. “The test should be the scale and severity of the impact, rather than whether the failure looks technically dramatic.”

On the other hand, he added, “An AI near-miss is an event that could realistically have caused serious harm, but was caught before that harm occurred. For example, an AI agent might attempt an unauthorized transfer that a separate approval control blocks, or a prompt-injection attack might induce it to disclose sensitive information, only for an outbound security control to stop the disclosure.”

However, Arntz warned of the risk to Rusu’s approach, should the final penalties be underwhelming. “There is a risk of this becoming a paper tiger if compliance amounts to filing a report and absorbing a predictable fine,” he said. 

Warnings from multiple directions

UK-based Gartner VP analyst Nader Henein said he is skeptical about the significance of the FCA’s proposal, in part because so many UK enterprises already have to comply with EU regulations, which have started asking companies to make such disclosures.

“Financial watchdogs including the Bank of England (BoE), the UAE Central Bank, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore have all issued warnings,” he said. “A few months ago, the European central banks, together with the European Systemic Risk Board, escalated the cyber risk assessment level associated with frontier models to ‘severe,’ warning that simultaneous cyber incidents could impact the financial sector. They acknowledged that AI-driven cyber incidents now threaten core financial sector stability.”

Henein said that he is especially skeptical that meaningful changes will occur in the financial sector.

“Financial institutions tend to heed the warnings of the regulator that decides whether they can continue to operate, but without clear laws, regulatory oversight, and the obligatory fines, these disjointed statements are not likely to make a difference,” he said. 

Could ‘incentivize the wrong behavior’

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, added that one risk of this increased visibility requirement is that it could inadvertently incentivize the wrong behavior. 

“A bank with good monitoring may catch hundreds of attempts by AI agents to act outside their authority,” he said. “A bank with poor monitoring may report zero, because it never saw them. On paper, the safer bank looks worse. A model failing a red-team test is the test working, not a regulatory incident.”

However, Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, said that the near-miss approach has the strongest potential to change the conversation.

“I love the near-miss idea. It is the most important thing in the speech. It is the part financial firms are least ready for,” he said. 

But, he stressed, “[Rusu] also warns about reliance on a single model. An outage at one AI supplier that takes down a customer service channel counts, too.”

Another concern about reliance on a specific model is the ever-present risk that an AI vendor could change the model without telling all of its customers. 

“A model can pass testing in March and misbehave in May without anyone at the firm changing a line of code, because the provider changed the model underneath,” Dickson said. “A model version change should get the same scrutiny as any other production change.”

item.title: The inference path is where AI value is won or lost
item.description:
As organizations incorporate AI into their environments, they’re hyper-focused on the AI model. Many executives I talk to spend a lot of time considering what model they should purchase from which vendor. They’re also concerned about which use case they should implement first.

Yet the reality is that AI models are swappable components. The vast majority of organizations are using multiple AI models, switching them out for their specific needs based on cost, accuracy, and security. It’s the right thing to do; organizations with architectures that make it difficult to swap out AI models are making the wrong bet.

What can’t be swapped out is your inference path—or everything that happens between a user’s intent and the model’s output. This includes the retrieval layer that decides what context the model sees. It includes the routing logic that chooses what model handles which request. It includes the identity that travels with the call. And it includes your organization’s policies, which decide what the model can do with the answer. That is where accuracy and costs are determined. It’s also where your proprietary advantage lies. A competitor can buy the same model you have, but they cannot buy your inference path, which determines not only the quality and cost of AI, but also its performance, resilience, and security at scale.

Adoption of AI inference is outpacing readiness

That truth is becoming increasingly important as AI adoption continues to accelerate. Recent F5 research found that more than three of every four organizations (78%) now run AI inference themselves across an average of seven AI models. Yet our research from a year ago found that just 2% of organizations were genuinely equipped to operate AI at scale.

What this shows is that enterprises are taking inference in-house, even when they’re not ready, because they want their data, expenses, and security posture under their own roof. All of this makes sense. But taking inference in-house also means taking responsibility for every decision, control, and dependency surrounding it. That is a much larger operational commitment than simply procuring a model.

The challenge of securing the inference path

Managing the inference path is not simply an AI security problem. It’s an application delivery, security, and operations challenge that spans the entire hybrid multicloud environment. As organizations move from pilots to production, every additional model, application, agent, API, and deployment environment adds another potential point of latency, policy inconsistency, or exposure. Today, 86% of enterprises operate across hybrid multicloud environments, and their inference path runs through all of it. As they add more AI models, applications, and agents, the number of possible inference paths multiplies, as do the performance and security challenges.

Let’s assume you’re a company with multiple AI models, with each step 95% reliable—a generous assumption for anything involving retrieval, tool calls, and a probabilistic model. A three-step pilot chain succeeds 86% of the time. A 20-step production chain succeeds 36% of the time. As you add more steps, the system will go from mostly fine to mostly broken.

When it comes to security, if each agent in a chain has a 5% chance of being manipulated, mis-scoped, or handed a credential it should not have, with a 20-agent workflow there’s a very strong chance that at least one link is exploitable. This is why more than nine out of 10 organizations report new categories of problems once agentic AI hits production levels, according to our research, including credential handling, action auditing, and the basic question of what an agent did on whose authority.

Tips for managing your inference path

So how can enterprises manage the inference path? Here are three points to consider as you get started:

  • Get a better handle on your AI infrastructure: You need to know many models your organization has in production and how long it takes to add or replace one. You need to know the longest agent chain in production and its measured end-to-end success rate. You need to know how AI policy is enforced and what’s required to update it. And you need to know what percentage of inference latency is due to security and governance overhead. Comprehending all of this is key to sound management.
  • Treat performance, security, and governance as a single priority. While enterprises have historically viewed the three as separate priorities, AI collapses them into one budget that’s measured in milliseconds and tokens.Every guardrail you add to the inference path results in more latency. Every governance requirement costs context window, which costs money on every single call. Prompt inspection, output filtering, PII redaction, model routing, retry logic: each is simultaneously a security control, a performance cost, and a line item. You can’t fund one without taking budget from the others, and you can’t cut one without exposing the rest.
  • Simplify complexity with a platform approach. The average enterprise today uses seven AI models, operates in multiple clouds, and maintains applications and APIs spread across on-premises, public clouds, and colocation environments. Applying policies separately across every model, environment, and protocol creates inconsistency, blind spots, and unnecessary operational work. Using an array of point solutions makes it extremely difficult to apply consistent policies or know which control is responsible when something goes wrong. A single enforcement point is critical, regardless of the model, environment, or protocol used.

A platform approach brings delivery, security, and governance together so organizations can enforce policies more consistently, maintain visibility across the inference path, and change models or infrastructure without rebuilding their controls each time. This helps enterprises scale AI while preserving performance, resilience, and operational choice.

 The F5 Application Delivery and Security Platform (ADSP) provides enterprise-grade visibility, governance, and protection for AI applications, models, agents, and APIs across today’s complex infrastructures. To learn more, visit the F5 ADSP webpage.

As Chief Product Officer at F5, Kunal Anand leads product vision, strategy, and execution—ensuring the development of breakthrough solutions that solve critical challenges and create exceptional experiences for customers. item.title: SAP must stop infringing a Celonis process mining patent, court rules
item.description:
The legal disputes between Germany’s largest software company, SAP, and the Munich-based process mining specialist Celonis took another turn last week. After the German Federal Cartel Office most recently dismissed a complaint filed by Celonis in July, the Munich I Regional Court ruled entirely in favor of Celonis in a case regarding the infringement of a European patent held by Celonis.

Case No. 7 O 12849/25 concerned patent EP 3 139 274 B1 describing a method for determining a net lead time between process steps using process data stored in a structured manner in main memory (in-memory).

Celonis had filed a lawsuit alleging that the patent was infringed by a feature of the SAP Signavio Process Intelligence software solution — SAP acquired Celonis’s rival Signavio in March 2021.

SAP must cease use and provide information

The court ruling prohibits SAP from offering the patent-protected method in Germany or using it itself. SAP must also provide Celonis with information regarding the extent to which it has infringed the patent since April 22, 2020, including details on:

  • where the patent-infringing processes originated and through which channels they were offered and distributed;
  • which customers purchased them, including names and addresses;
  • how many access licenses were granted and how much users paid for them;
  • for how many users the methods were used per calendar year;
  • which other individuals were involved in offering and using the methods.

In addition, SAP must provide a transparent account of the extent of the patent infringements based on its financial figures. The company is obligated to pay appropriate compensation or damages.

“The ruling by the Munich Regional Court confirms our legal position: SAP Signavio’s technology infringes on Celonis’s patent rights. We consistently protect our intellectual property and remain committed to fair competition,” explained a Celonis spokesperson.

SAP says no consequences for its customers

SAP, however, points out that the court ruling pertains to a single, specific feature within SAP Signavio Process Intelligence, not to the product as a whole. SAP Signavio Process Intelligence remains available to customers, according to a company spokesperson.

The spokesperson also dismissed concerns that the ruling could hinder companies’ migration to SAP S/4HANA Cloud. Migrations to SAP S/4HANA Cloud are not affected by this, he said. SAP is working to ensure that there are no disruptions for its customers.

The concern is not entirely unfounded: SAP Signavio is part of Rise with SAP, a SaaS solution from the Walldorf-based company designed to support migration to the S/4HANA Cloud. SAP Signavio’s process mining tools are designed to provide insight into actual process flows and identify inefficiencies and bottlenecks.

SAP will appeal

The Regional Court’s ruling does not mean the matter is by any means settled: As the spokesperson for the Walldorf-based software giant explained, SAP does not share the Munich court’s legal opinion and will file an appeal against the ruling. In addition, SAP has challenged the validity of the patent in question before the Federal Patent Court.

“SAP’s top priority is to ensure that customers are not affected by this. All other issues will be resolved through the appropriate legal channels,” said the spokesperson for the Walldorf-based company.

This article first appeared on Computerwoche on Oct. 13, 2026.

item.title: CIO 100 Leadership Live Chicago: CIOs reassess AI economics, governance, and leadership
item.description:
Artificial intelligence is forcing CIOs to reconsider the economics of enterprise technology. While application development costs are falling, autonomous systems are complicating governance as traditional productivity measures struggle to capture returns on transformation investments for C-suite executives and boards of directors who are interested in documenting tangible business gains from agentic deployments.

These were among the issues that dominated CIO 100 Leadership Live Chicago on Oct. 13, where enterprise technology executives, industry specialists and investors examined the practical implications of moving AI from experimentation into everyday business operations.

Speakers repeatedly observed that technological innovation is outpacing the ability of traditional enterprise processes to absorb it. The theme surfaced first in the opening panel, “Championing Tech-Enabled Business Transformation,” moderated by Dan Roberts, host of the Tech Whisperers podcast.

Laura Walsh, CIO of Culligan, described the conflicting expectations technology leaders face. They are asked to accelerate AI adoption, demonstrate immediate financial returns, maintain security and quality, and fund new initiatives within existing budgets.

Walsh stressed the importance of established management disciplines, including data governance, project execution and technology business management. She outlined a hub-and-spoke approach that establishes common AI controls while allowing individual business units to experiment.

Jamie Head, founder and CEO of Stack360, contended that CIOs must work more closely with CEOs and CFOs to identify a limited number of strategic priorities and decide which initiatives to defer. Business leaders, he added, increasingly look to automation to improve margins and productivity, creating an imperative for CIOs to play a key role in separating worthwhile investments from technological distractions.

AI economics move beyond productivity

The financial implications of AI adoption surfaced throughout the day, particularly the gap between gains in employee productivity and measurable financial returns.

In a discussion of the intelligent enterprise moderated by Jon Glick, principal and advisory CMO at PwC, PwC principal Scott Behrens said AI transformation requires redesigning business processes from the ground up. Organizations that layer disconnected AI applications onto existing workflows risk increasing technology consumption without corresponding business benefits, he warned.

Meghna Shah, principal for engineering and AI at PwC, pointed to the widening gap between the speed of AI-assisted software development and the engineering discipline required to deploy reliable enterprise applications. AI can dramatically accelerate prototyping, she noted, but organizations must still address architecture, integration, security and quality assurance before those applications can support critical business operations.

Andy Xydakis, global CIO of Aon, said the company has expanded its cloud footprint from about 35% to 85% of its application portfolio while introducing AI capabilities to roughly 60,000 employees. AI-assisted proposal development has cut work that once required 40 to 50 hours to about four or five hours, according to Xydakis. Aon has also strengthened its financial operations capabilities to monitor technology consumption and manage costs as adoption expands.

A subsequent session examined how to secure returns on transformation investments in emerging technologies such as AI. Chris Campbell, CIO of DeVry University, said that his team measures investments against broad institutional objectives, including student enrollment, persistence, retention and graduation rates, in addition to savings from individual technology projects.

Campbell also maintained that CIOs must understand the business capabilities their organizations need before choosing applications or technologies. AI is making software development more accessible, he noted, so technology leaders must work with business stakeholders to set common priorities and guardrails while managing expectations about what emerging technologies can realistically accomplish.

Prashant Shanti Kumar, global head of data domains at Marsh, recommended setting clear business objectives and breaking complex transformation initiatives into manageable phases. Drawing on his experience integrating organizations and business processes, including at a major national insurance carrier, Kumar advocated 90-day implementation plans with measurable outcomes that let teams adjust priorities as conditions change.

Gone, both intimated, are the days of multi-year strategic technology and deployment plans.

Distributed development raises governance challenges

As the economics of enterprise technology grow more complicated as the result of increasing numbers of autonomous agents and applications, Michael Blank, chief operating officer of Retool, said AI is dramatically reducing the cost of generating software while leaving enterprises responsible for the infrastructure, maintenance, security and governance required to run it.

Blank warned that business employees can now build applications without IT’s knowledge, creating operational dependencies and exposing information to poorly governed systems. He recommended allowing development throughout the organization under consistent enterprise controls over identities, permissions, data access and application deployment.

The growing autonomy of AI systems is also forcing cybersecurity leaders to rethink traditional protection strategies, the focus of a security and risk panel moderated by CIO contributor Joan Goodchild.

Heather Ceylan, chief information security officer at Box, said organizations must monitor and restrict what an AI agent actually does, in addition to controlling which resources it can access. Agents may operate with broad permissions, process large volumes of sensitive information and execute actions far faster than human employees, she explained. Ceylan said security controls therefore need to operate during execution, when potentially harmful behavior can be identified and interrupted.

Ceylan described using security agents to review code, perform threat modeling and help enforce engineering requirements as software development accelerates.

Greg Sylvester, vice president of enterprise AI and infrastructure at Cisco, discussed the importance of monitoring agent activity, detecting malicious instructions and building responsible AI requirements directly into enterprise platforms.

Michael Chahino, CIO of Elgin Community College, outlined additional challenges facing higher education, where decentralized decision-making and widespread use of personal AI subscriptions complicate governance. His institution is emphasizing education and cross-functional oversight while developing policies for responsible AI use.

The discussion pointed to a broader need for greater visibility into the behavior of autonomous systems and clearer accountability for their decisions as those systems gain the ability to communicate and act independently.

Legacy systems and data remain critical

Several speakers stressed that AI transformation depends on the quality of existing enterprise systems and information. The issue received detailed attention in the “Modernizing the Enterprise Application Estate” session, moderated by Woody Evans, vice president of global solutions engineering at Perforce Delphix.

Ron Guerrier, chief technology officer of Save the Children, warned that AI-generated applications can create substantial operational risks when business teams expect prototypes to move directly into production. He advocated established engineering practices and continuous improvement principles, along with investment in employees who understand the organization’s technology environment and business processes.

Deepak Gangwaar, senior vice president at Northern Trust, highlighted the importance of reliable, accessible test data and appropriate compliance controls. Faster code generation offers limited benefits if developers must still wait for suitable data to validate applications, he noted.

Panelists also explored AI’s potential to help organizations analyze legacy code, understand embedded business logic and identify modernization opportunities.

Guerrier cautioned that enterprises must weigh the full economics of modernization, including ongoing infrastructure expenses, AI consumption costs and long-term vendor commitments.

CIOs reconsider how they invest

Uncertainty in AI technology markets prompted a discussion of whether CIOs should adopt some of the investment practices venture capital firms use.

Mike Asem, founding partner at M25, and Gale Wilkinson, founder and managing partner of Vitalize, said organizations can benefit from testing promising technologies through structured pilot programs with defined objectives and acceptable levels of risk.

Asem pointed to the opportunity cost of avoiding emerging technologies and the value of validating assumptions before committing substantial resources.

Wilkinson described growing investor interest in specialized AI applications that address specific business processes. She suggested that enterprises can gain by working with early-stage technology companies as design partners, helping shape solutions around operational requirements.

Their remarks highlighted the need to balance governance and risk management against the possibility that excessive caution could leave organizations behind competitors.

Leadership and workforce development take center stage

The conference closed with a discussion of how CIO responsibilities may evolve over the next 12 to 24 months.

Samir Shah, senior vice president and global CIO of Brunswick Corp., described an AI operating model in which business executives identify priority processes, commit funding and take responsibility for financial outcomes.

Shah said Brunswick has generated about $8 million to $10 million in tangible savings over the past 18 months. The company is pursuing a portfolio of 18 to 20 AI use cases across areas including supply chain operations, customer service, pricing and software development, with more than $50 million in targeted value.

Darlene Reina, director of IT and AI enablement at Babylist, said her organization is giving business employees the tools and guardrails to build applications themselves, freeing IT specialists to concentrate on higher-value initiatives and production requirements.

Reina also addressed the workforce implications of AI adoption. As routine technology tasks become automated, she said, organizations must prepare existing employees for new responsibilities and rethink how they recruit and develop entry-level talent.

She advocated retraining and redeploying employees whose responsibilities are changing, noting that their knowledge of business operations remains valuable as technology capabilities evolve.

Speakers throughout the day identified financial discipline, governance, sound technical foundations and workforce development as the requirements for sustaining AI-driven transformation as the technology continues to evolve.

item.title: AI agents are joining the workforce, so it’s time to rethink the business plan
item.description:
Enterprise AI is racing toward a consequential shift in how businesses operate. As agents take on work that used to consume the week, projects once dismissed as ‘we don’t have the capacity’ become worth another look. That raises a question worth bringing into the next planning meeting: What would we pursue if our teams had more time to do it?

Most organizations already have an answer. There are customers who deserve more attention, promising ideas waiting for someone to develop them, and services that would be valuable if the economics made sense. These opportunities often stay out of the business plan because the people needed to pursue them are already fully committed.

AI gives leaders a reason to revisit those decisions. As AI becomes more widely adopted, simply deploying agents will not be enough to differentiate one organization from another. The bigger opportunity is to rethink how the business operates, which customer needs it can address and where it can create value that wasn’t previously possible.

The State of Enterprise AI Adoption Report, published by Creatio based on a survey of 608 IT and business decision-makers, shows how widely that possibility is taking shape. Seventy percent of respondents say their organizations have moved beyond AI experimentation. Meanwhile, 78% are already scaling AI agents across departments or use cases, or expect to within a year. As that adoption expands, the opportunity is to connect additional capacity to a more ambitious business plan.

Put the work you postponed back on the agenda

One of the report’s most revealing findings concerns workforce expectations. Eighty-nine percent of respondents expect AI agents to augment teams, expand capacity or create new roles. Only 9% anticipate significant headcount reductions. These expectations do not establish what will ultimately happen to employment, but they show how many organizations are thinking about AI’s potential.

The interesting management decision is what happens to the capacity they expect to gain.

A service team might use it to give complex customer problems more attention. A sales organization might finally have the resources to support accounts that previously received little engagement. An operations team might tackle a persistent backlog while keeping pace with new requests. Each possibility needs a business case, but AI can change the assumptions that made the work difficult to justify.

I would make that discussion part of every significant AI investment. Alongside the estimate of hours saved, ask what those hours could make possible. Give the business owner responsibility for explaining how the team will use the capacity and how customers or employees will benefit. That makes the investment much easier to connect to a growth priority.

A faster task should help the whole business move forward

Additional capacity depends on how well AI fits into the work around it. Consider customer onboarding. An agent might gather information, identify missing documents and prepare an application for review. That can reduce administrative effort considerably. But the customer’s experience also depends on what happens next: whether the application reaches the right person, whether exceptions are resolved promptly and whether the customer has to provide the same information again.

The opportunity is to improve that entire experience. Employees can focus on decisions that require judgment, supported by information the agent has already organized. With a well-designed handoff, the business may be able to onboard more customers while giving each one appropriate attention.

This is why I would treat workflow design as a business leadership responsibility. Technology teams can establish what an agent can do. The people who run the process can explain where that capability would make a meaningful difference. Bringing those perspectives together helps organizations choose useful applications and define how responsibility should pass between people and agents.

Employees should have a voice in that design. They know which exceptions occur every week, where information is unreliable and which seemingly simple tasks require careful judgment. Their experience can make an AI deployment better from the outset. Involving them also creates a practical setting for learning how to direct agents and evaluate their work.

Give teams the confidence to expand

As agents take on more responsibility, clear governance makes expansion easier to manage. The report finds that 71% of respondents with fully established AI governance feel very confident about scaling AI, compared with 17% of those still developing a framework.

That is an association, rather than proof that governance alone creates confidence. Still, it offers a useful perspective on a subject often discussed mainly in terms of restrictions. Clear authority can help people move faster because they understand which decisions they are empowered to make.

The same principle applies to agents. An agent preparing a summary needs different permissions from one making changes to a customer account. Teams should know what each agent can access, which actions require approval and how to intervene when necessary. A business owner should be responsible for reviewing performance as the process evolves.

Once those practices are established, other teams can build on them. Every deployment becomes an opportunity to develop approaches that the next team can reuse, reducing the effort required to expand AI across the organization. Governance becomes part of the organization’s ability to execute consistently.

Make the business case bigger than hours saved

The report also gives leaders a reason to broaden how they evaluate AI’s contribution. Among organizations automating more than half of their workflows with AI, 33% report increased revenue from AI in the previous six months. Among those automating less than 10%, the figure is 14%.

Those percentages describe how many organizations reported a benefit, not how much their revenue increased. Nor do they guarantee that automating more workflows will produce growth. They do, however, suggest that deeper adoption deserves consideration as part of the revenue conversation.

Hours saved are a useful starting point. The more revealing question is what changed for the business.

For a customer service initiative, that could mean resolving more issues successfully while maintaining customer satisfaction. In sales, it could mean increasing the time available for customer engagement and examining whether that contributes to stronger conversion or retention. Connecting operational measures to business outcomes helps leaders decide where to invest next.

There is room to improve that connection. Among respondents pursuing AI to improve customer experience, only 56% measure customer satisfaction. Agreeing on the intended outcome and its measure before deployment would give these organizations a clearer basis for assessing progress. It would also help teams refine their approach as they learn.

Revisit the assumptions behind the plan

Business plans reflect assumptions about what an organization can deliver with the people and resources it has. As AI changes that capacity, those assumptions deserve another look.

Some opportunities will still be constrained by demand, funding or factors that AI cannot resolve. Others may become much more achievable. Leadership teams should be willing to reopen the discussion, particularly around work they postponed because employees lacked the time to pursue it.

That is what makes this stage of enterprise AI so consequential. The opportunity extends beyond freeing up employees’ time or making existing processes more efficient. AI gives organizations a chance to rethink how they operate, how they serve customers and which business opportunities they can pursue.

As AI adoption becomes increasingly widespread, deploying AI agents alone will not create a lasting competitive advantage. What will differentiate organizations is how effectively they use AI to reinvent their business models, redesign processes and deliver better customer experiences.

The competitive advantage of the AI era won’t come from simply adopting AI. It will come from reimagining what’s possible with it.

item.title: CIOs look to accelerate digital transformation with AI
item.description:
IT leaders seeking promising AI use cases may be overlooking a potential goldmine: deploying the technology to assist with major IT modernization and digital transformation initiatives.

Leading CIOs at a handful of large enterprises have leveraged generative AI and related tools to rewrite code, redesign workflows, and migrate databases during major digital transformation efforts, a practice that isn’t as widespread as its potential suggests.

“The potential is actually, I don’t want to say ‘limitless,’ but it is,” says Vijay Thangella, head of AI and machine learning at contact center technology provider Avaya. “There’s a very high potential.”

Avaya, using AI tools built from frontier models, claims it can help customers cut contact-center modernization timelines drastically. Revamping legacy contact centers typically requires IT teams to spend months deciphering and manually rebuilding years of workflows, routing logic, integrations, and business rules. AI-assisted modernization can cut the time to a few days, Thangella says.

Managed services provider Ensono also uses AI tools to help customers with tasks such as code discovery and cleaning up legacy code. While most organizations still haven’t used AI to assist with digital transformation, the technology can significantly cut the costs and time associated with large IT modernization projects, says Brian Klingbeil, chief strategy officer at the company.

An emerging sweet spot for digital transformation

Gartner AI analyst Arun Chandrasekaran sees significant potential to accelerate digital transformation initiatives through use of generative AI and related tools, in particular for gathering requirements, mapping legacy code, and performing code quality assurance.

“There’s a lot of interest out there today, but customers are not fully there yet,” he says. “The models are getting better at a lot of these tasks, but they are still often hindered by hallucination rates.”

In many cases, CIOs are still working to improve their organizations’ AI governance and data infrastructure, two foundational steps they must take before their teams can use AI to assist with digital transformation, Chandrasekaran adds.

Interest in the concept is high among CIOs of midsize companies, who often have limited budgets to commit to large-scale, multi-year digital transformation projects and a higher comfort level with risk than IT leaders at multibillion-dollar multinational enterprises, he says.

“It seems like you need to accept or tolerate a certain level of risk to trust your AI to do some things that you were doing yourself,” Chandrasekaran adds.

Leading the charge

Rama Donepudi, SVP and global CIO at Mead Johnson Nutrition, is among the vanguard of IT leaders using AI to assist with digital transformation.

Back in 2024, Donepudi turned to a combination of gen AI and AI-enabled automation to assist with the baby formula maker’s transition from legacy SAP ERP to S/4HANA.

Donepudi’s IT team used gen AI coding copilots to remediate their custom programs for compatibility with the newer ERP package, and they used UiPath AI-enabled bots to automate data validation between the legacy environment and S/4HANA.

In addition, Donepudi’s team used AI-enabled tools such as Enable Now and WalkMe to support the development of training and other learning content development. They also deployed GPT tools to create program communications to employees throughout the transformation.

Gen AI was one tool in the toolbox, Donepudi notes. “We deliberately applied different AI capabilities across development, validation, training, and communications rather than treating AI as a single use case,” he says.

Using AI for content creation resulted in a significant cost savings, he says, and enabled the company to target content toward specific employee roles and make immediate changes as the project progressed.

“AI can generate all of this content if I give it the right prompts, and everything becomes easier,” he says. “My change management overall become easier.”

The benefits of AI were significant, Donepudi adds. Without using AI tools, the company projected the modernization project to take 17 to 18 months, but by using AI, it completed the project in 11 months. The cost savings from the compressed timeline added up to between $5 million and $6 million, he says.

“We went down on Friday evening,” Donepudi told his CIO peers at this year’s CIO 100 Awards and Conference in August of the company’s final transition. “Monday morning the business came back and they were like, Rama, are we on S/4 now? Yes, we are on S/4. They didn’t even realize that we were able to do all of that. That’s the beauty of using AI extensively in our training and testing, documenting. We showed them what AI can do. That’s our story.”

While Donepudi believes there is great potential for AI in digital transformation projects, he also sees hesitation among his peers. As Gartner’s Chandrasekaran observed, many larger organizations don’t have the same risk/reward tolerance that Mead Johnson Nutrition was comfortable with, he says.

In addition, big consulting firms still have fans among the CIO set, Donepudi adds.

“The reason we engage all these big consulting forms primarily is for that program management, change management, comms management, all of that handholding,” he says. “Where these Deloittes, IBMs, and Accentures come into the picture is that they know how to do these large transformations, and you’re touching your entire company — finance, supply, procurement, and sales — and they help navigate the change.”

But for CIOs willing to take a risk, the rewards can be great, Donepudi says.

“It’s a new approach and it’s risky, and I am taking full ownership,” he says. “I’m fully accountable for this one versus, ‘I gave this deployment to IBM for $50 million per year, and it’s on IBM to help us if something goes wrong. IBM is on the hook.’”

The project also gave Donepudi the opportunity to inspire the rest of his organization to trust in the power of AI, he says.

“If I don’t walk the walk of using AI department, how can I go tell my finance, supply, or marketing guys to use AI because it gives you productivity, it gives you an efficiency?” he says. “I took the risk at the end, and it paid off for me.”

item.title: Closing the agent governance gap
item.description:
The emerging challenge with AI agents isn’t simply preventing attacks from external rogue AI agents; it’s accounting for what your own agents are doing on the inside. AI agents are already rewiring how organizations operate, and we’re only in the first inning. Recent incidents, however, have exposed the risk for individuals and enterprises alike. This is happening because organizations are moving fast and pushing themselves to move even faster. 

In this environment, AI agents have created edge cases that reveal real risks when deployed without sufficient security controls. And further, no one can predict the impact of advances coming over the next six months. All of this reinforces the need to get security fundamentals right. If you’re building with AI agents right now, you know the real challenge isn’t just getting them to run. It’s knowing what happens when they act on their own. That starts with three questions. What agents do I have in my environment? What are they doing? And what are they capable of doing?

The proliferation problem

Agentic governance is problematic because enterprises must track a sprawling agent landscape AND ensure each agent is built and deployed securely. Also, agentic adoption is frictionless. Creating an agent is only one API call away from a model provider. Vibe coding means any curious employee can build an agent. This triple proliferation of vendor agents, platform native agents and homegrown agents compounds the problem. 

Visibility is the starting line

There is the famous security adage that you can’t protect what you can’t see. Right now, most organizations lack basic visibility into what agents are in their environments. According to Anthropic, 82 percent of organizations have discovered unregistered agents in their network, and 57 percent already deploy agents for multi-stage workflows.

In addition to basic visibility, enterprises also need to understand other related attributes, such as who onboarded the agents, what access privileges they have and how they are behaving as designed. For example, an over-provisioned agent, like an email agent with 50 tools attached, would be suspect and worth investigating.

Security teams also need one view of their agents across every platform they run on, because each platform has its own permissions and its own telemetry. When each agent has a single record, security teams can connect what it can do on one platform with what it can do on another, and compare both with what the agent was built to do. That’s how seemingly routine activities add up to an attack chain. An agent might read customer records in one cloud, hold a credential for a payments API in another and be able to send messages from a SaaS application. No single platform sees a problem, but together they form a path to move sensitive data out of the company that the agent’s intended scope never required. Similarly, an agent that gains permissions across several platforms over time might never trigger an alert in any one of them, yet the combined record shows how its reach has far exceeded its purpose.

Governance must extend from build-time to runtime

Shift-left security helps find model or tool vulnerabilities before deployment, to find risks before an agent goes into production. That’s a necessary first step, but insufficient. Agents create tightly coupled runtime behavior-to-vulnerability. Unlike traditional software, AI agents exhibit behaviors at runtime that can’t necessarily be predicted by inspecting the code in the development phase. Code analysis can’t uncover prompt hijacking, poisoned context or goal drift. 

The model has evolved from “secure the code, then ship it” to continuous behavioral oversight at execution time, layered on top of build-time governance. Pre-deployment security analysis is still required because spec-driven development enforces checkpoints before code is generated. But runtime monitoring is also necessary to detect exposures in the production environment and enforce what agents do versus what they’re scoped to do. 

In practice, this means applying two layers of control to every agent. The first layer is runtime behavioral boundaries. These define what an agent can do. They determine what the agent can reach, what it can return and where it must stop and ask for human approval. This is the enforcement mechanism that operationalizes runtime governance. The second layer is identity controls. These define what an agent is allowed to touch.

Think of every agent like a scoped, temporary employee with an expiration date. You enforce this by applying familiar IAM principles to agents. Least privilege. Short-lived credentials. Multi-factor authentication for long-lived credentials. Just like an individual contributor engineer shouldn’t get access to the broader team’s payroll, a code generation agent shouldn’t be provisioned to push directly to production environments. An agent designed to answer customer queries shouldn’t get read/write access to the customer database. An IT helpdesk agent doesn’t need domain admin privileges to alter security policies. 

Prioritize by exploitability, not severity

AI-fueled exploits are breaking down CVE-based severity scoring. The status quo is security teams patching the most critical vulnerabilities first. But attackers don’t always work that way. They can now use agents to chain low-severity vulnerabilities together in ways that render individual scores meaningless while building attack paths that combine for a devastating impact.

For example, an agent might combine an information disclosure flaw, a misconfigured service account and an unpatched privilege escalation into a single attack path that reaches sensitive data, even though none of those vulnerabilities would individually trigger an urgent patch cycle. If that path leads to customer PII or financial records, organizations face regulatory action under frameworks like GDPR, HIPAA or PCI DSS. If it exposes API keys, service credentials or internal network configurations, the attacker gains a foothold for lateral movement across the environment. 

Context is critical. A vulnerability in network-isolated code is much less dangerous than the same vulnerability in an internet-facing service. Rather than treating every vulnerability in isolation, the better approach is to prioritize based on exploitability within the actual runtime environment. Factor in what’s reachable, what damage an attacker could do and the business impact.

The new security fundamentals for agents 

The emerging challenge with AI agents is accounting for what your own agents are doing inside your enterprise. In this environment, enterprises need visibility, runtime governance and exploitability-based prioritization. To that end, the security fundamentals you already know still matter. You should already be applying least privilege, short-lived credentials, MFA for the necessary long-lived credentials, automated pipelines and proper testing to secure your corporate environment. These controls limit what an agent can access and what damage it can do if compromised. You will also want to add the agent-specific fundamentals mentioned earlier: visibility, continuous behavioral oversight, identity controls and exploitability-based prioritization. These capabilities tell you what your agents are doing, whether they should be taking those actions and how to intervene when they drift. Together, pre-agentic security fundamentals and agent-specific best practices provide the baseline governance guardrails to secure AI agents. 

Organizations that get this right can accelerate agentic deployments at scale, unlocking innovation while minimizing unintended consequences.

item.title: Meta’s new commercial terms say if its AI makes a mistake, it will legally be the customer’s fault
item.description:
In Meta commercial terms changes slated to kick in on October 30, the company will shift the liability for any mistakes made by its AI models to its enterprise customers. The new language also makes those IT executives responsible for anything done by a partner or contractor.

The changes also finally put a stake into the heart of robots.txt, with Meta granting itself the right to grab, and use for its own purposes, any content associated with a Meta account.

The language allows Meta to “use automated software such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs, and any content available through them, that are associated with your products or services,” according to the new language on its website on Monday. Meta also wants to be able to “periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content.”

Consultants said the three biggest concerns they had about the changes were the web scraping, data ownership, and AI liability transfer.

Web scraping and data ownership

However, Meta emailed a statement to CIO.com late Monday suggesting that it was rethinking its position on web scraping. Saying that Meta wanted “to clarify” the web scraping changes, Emil Vazques, a Meta public affairs manager, said, “the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

As of Monday evening, New York time, the proposed document’s wording had yet to be altered to reflect this, but Vazques said that a change was coming soon.

The data ownership issue sets Meta apart from other AI vendors in that it wants to train its models on anything it encounters. Then again, the nature of Meta businesses focuses on advertising and would therefore be expected to seek more data control.

The new proposed phrasing, which Meta could alter before it takes effect later this month, said that using any Meta product grants Meta “a license to content that is covered by intellectual property rights like photos or videos you share, post, or upload on or in connection with our Meta Company Products. That license applies to content you or someone on your behalf, such as your agency that places an ad for you or your service provider that manages your Page content for you, makes available on or in connection with any Meta Company Products. Without limiting anything in our terms and for clarity, Meta may use such content … to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain Meta Company Products.”

AI liability

But the change that prompted the most raised eyebrows involved AI liabilities. 

The proposed language said, “AI features may make mistakes and may not always produce accurate, complete, or suitable results,” and customers “are solely responsible for and assume any and all risks associated with such AI features and any resulting content.”

That AI clause, said Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, “turns accountability upside down. Meta builds the AI features, admits they ‘may make mistakes’ and then assigns ‘any and all risks’ to the business.”

Mike Wilkes, enterprise CISO at Aikido Security, agreed that the move is perplexing.

“The new AI provisions shift substantial responsibility for inaccurate or unsuitable outputs onto customers. That makes no sense,” he said. “As an example, the ASPCA is going to be liable for Meta creating unsuitable results when they ask Meta to create an image of a dog. Only Meta has control of the model being used to create that image. I see a very high flight risk among enterprise customers when platforms impose such onerous terms and conditions around content usage.”

The October 30 date that the US-based Meta chose is ironic. That is the day before Halloween, which is known as mischief night in the US, when children play pranks on their neighbors. Given that, Dickson said, the date for these changes is appropriate: “Meta is handing out the tricks and keeping the treats.” 

He added that the data grab is frightening. “What Meta wants is content: what a business posts, uploads, or shares on or in connection with Meta’s products,” he noted. “The trouble is the phrase ‘in connection with,’ which can stretch as far as Meta needs it to. The list of ‘Meta Company Products’ lives on a separate page that Meta can revise at will. The license grows every time that list does.”

And, Dickson noted: “Meta may use the content to ‘provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain’ its products. Those five verbs cover nearly everything a technology company does.”

‘Legal sophistry’

One of the obvious defensive measures for an enterprise is to sever all relations with Meta. But beyond the pragmatic difficulties of doing that, given the powerful market share enjoyed by Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram and Threads, such a move may not even solve the problem. That is because Meta made other contract changes in July that make Meta licenses “perpetual” and that said, “this license survives termination of these terms by any party for any reason.”

That, said Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, means that the “the general content license ends when content is deleted from Meta’s systems,” not when the enterprise ends a contract.

One additional twist to the new language is that Meta had recently tweaked it to no longer explicitly say that it would train it models on enterprise data. But Thomas Randall, a research director at Infotech, said that the wording change made by Meta amounted to legal sophistry. “The revised version drops the word ‘train’ and states that collection is just for developing and maintaining advertising and business products, alongside protecting Meta products’ integrity and security.”

But dropping the word “train” is “not a substantive fix,” he pointed out. “The revised terms are still flexible enough to cover most AI work. When combined with other aspects of the revised terms — continued use equals consent, broad indemnity, AS-IS disclaimer, and Meta’s freedom to discontinue products without notice or liability — this is a one-way street. The difference between ‘train Meta products’ and ‘developing and maintaining Meta products’ is a matter of how you pronounce tomato.”

Could force IT strategy changes

In addition, Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, stressed that this contract could be an industry admission that robots.txt no longer delivers any meaningful protections. Agentic systems had already made robots.txt close to irrelevant. 

“October 30 ends a thirty-year assumption that robots.txt protects what you publish. It never did,” Mahapatra said. “It was a courtesy convention the web agreed to honor, and Meta’s own framing of robots.txt as a place for site owners to register preferences tells you exactly how it will be weighed against a signed contract.”

Mahapatra said the language in the new Meta commercial terms could force a significant change in IT strategy.

“‘On your behalf’ extends the license to whatever your agencies and vendors upload. ‘Associated’ extends the crawl to domains nobody has defined, including the ones where marketing pages sit beside product documentation, research, and investor materials,” Mahapatra said. “Most CIOs cannot tell me how many Meta pages, ad accounts, and WhatsApp numbers carry their brand, because marketing and agencies own them and IT never inventoried them.”
